84-355 Democracy’s Data | The modifiable areal unit problem, on one county’s census blocks

Everything here runs as given. You will not write any code. Your job is to read what comes out and say what it means.

Read areal-units-brief.Rmd first. This lab runs the same numbered steps with the code exposed. The chunks that compute are shown; the chunks that only draw are folded away, because their job is pictures, not arithmetic.

The claim under examination

“Fulton County, Georgia is 44.8% Black.”

True. Also a fact about a shape somebody drew. This lab holds the census fixed — one day, one count, 1,066,710 people — and changes only the shape.

Two effects, and the whole lab depends on keeping them apart:

  • Scale effect — same points, bigger boxes. Blocks to block groups to tracts to counties.
  • Zoning effect — same number of boxes, same size boxes, different shapes. This is what redistricting is.

Step 1 — The same people, all the way down

c(ga_blocks   = FN("ga_blocks"),
  ga_pop      = FN("ga_pop"),
  ful_blocks  = FN("ful_blocks"),
  ful_blocks_with_people = FN("ful_blocks_pop"),
  ful_pop     = FN("ful_pop"),
  ful_black   = FN("ful_black"))
#>              ga_blocks                 ga_pop             ful_blocks 
#>                 232717               10711908                  11748 
#> ful_blocks_with_people                ful_pop              ful_black 
#>                   8674                1066710                 477624
c(ful_black_pct = FN("ful_black_pct"), ful_black_vap_pct = FN("ful_bvap_pct"))
#>     ful_black_pct ful_black_vap_pct 
#>             44.78             43.51

1,066,710 people on 11,748 blocks, of which 8,674 have anyone living on them. “Black” here means any part Black — any of the 32 of the census’s 63 race combinations that include Black or African American, which is the definition voting-rights litigation uses.

Every statistic below is population-weighted, so a block holding three people does not count as much as a tract holding six thousand.

Step 2 — Census geography is a string, not a map

eg <- mv[mv$lev == "b", ]
eg <- eg$unit[which.max(eg$pop)]      # the most populous Fulton block
c(block = eg, block_group = substr(eg, 1, 12), tract = substr(eg, 1, 11),
  county = substr(eg, 1, 5), state = substr(eg, 1, 2))
#>             block       block_group             tract            county 
#> "131210007002000"    "131210007002"     "13121000700"           "13121" 
#>             state 
#>              "13"

Climbing the census hierarchy is substr(). No overlay, no intersection, no interior points, no assumption about how people are spread inside a polygon. So nothing that changes in Steps 3–5 can be blamed on a geometric approximation: there isn’t one.

GEOIDs are character. Read that block as a number and it becomes 1.312101e+14; read a tract as a number and it silently loses its leading zero. Every read in this document that touches an identifier pins the column.

Step 3 — The scale effect, seen

8,674 shapes on the left, one shape on the right, exactly the same 1,066,710 people.

Step 4 — The scale effect, measured

lf[, c("level", "units", "median_pop", "mean_share", "sd_share",
       "p10_share", "p90_share", "units_majority")]
Level Units Median pop Mean share Sd share P10 share P90 share Units majority
Census block 8674 56 44.77543 37.92444 4.140127 97.41379 4129
Block group 856 1151 44.77543 36.69931 6.038201 95.45859 361
Census tract 326 3174 44.77543 36.17960 7.184579 95.15784 135
County 1 1066710 44.77543 0.00000 44.775431 44.77543 0

The mean is constant at 44.78% on every rung — it has to be, the same people are being averaged. That is the control. Everything else moves:

c(sd_blocks = LF("Census block", "sd_share"),
  sd_tracts = LF("Census tract", "sd_share"),
  sd_county = LF("County", "sd_share"),
  p10_blocks = LF("Census block", "p10_share"),
  p10_tracts = LF("Census tract", "p10_share"),
  p90_blocks = LF("Census block", "p90_share"),
  p90_tracts = LF("Census tract", "p90_share"))
#>  sd_blocks  sd_tracts  sd_county p10_blocks p10_tracts p90_blocks p90_tracts 
#>  37.924444  36.179603   0.000000   4.140127   7.184579  97.413793  95.157838

Statewide the same climb goes further, because Georgia contains between-county variation that Fulton cannot:

ls_ga[, c("level", "units", "sd_share", "max_share", "units_majority",
          "pct_black_in_majority", "corr_child")]
Level Units Sd share Max share Units majority Pct black in majority Corr child
Census block 165333 31.76072 100.00000 39309 66.33016 0.0882043
Block group 7433 28.40355 99.58621 2070 58.68384 0.0968917
Census tract 2784 27.07374 98.72674 723 55.44737 0.0801182
County 159 17.69965 72.69981 22 34.82968 -0.1467985

Two results in that table are worth stopping for.

No county in Georgia is as Black as thousands of its blocks are: 100.0% falls to 72.7%. And the share of Black Georgians who live in a majority-Black unit falls from 66.3% (blocks) to 55.4% (tracts) to 34.8% (counties). Nobody moved.

The correlation with the under-18 share changes sign — 0.088 across blocks, -0.147 across counties. A correlation is a fact about people and the boxes you sorted them into.

Step 5 — Watch the distribution collapse

Two humps, and they stay two humps. Fulton is segregated at a spatial scale larger than a census tract, so climbing three rungs barely touches it. The textbook version of the scale effect promises smooth collapse; this is a counterexample, and the reason is worth holding on to: how much the scale effect bites depends on how big the real spatial structure is compared with the unit.

Step 6 — The zoning effect: same size units, different shapes

Fulton elects a Board of Commissioners from 6 districts. So take the same blocks and cut them into 6 units of 177,785 people each — 360 different ways, from two rules, each rotated through 180 one-degree steps. Neither rule can see race.

c(plans = nrow(sm), units_per_plan = FN("K"), people_per_unit = FN("quota"),
  worst_population_deviation_pct = max(sm$max_dev_pct))
#>                          plans                 units_per_plan 
#>                        360.000                          6.000 
#>                people_per_unit worst_population_deviation_pct 
#>                     177785.000                          0.706
table(family = sm$family, majority_Black_units = sm$n_majority)
#>        majority_Black_units
#> family    0   1   2   3   4
#>   split   0   0 120  51   9
#>   strip   3  10 107  60   0

0 to 4. 3 plans put no unit over 50%. 9 put four over. 227 land on exactly two.

Step 7 — The two extremes, unit by unit

z <- pu[pu$plan %in% c("fewest", "most"),
        c("plan", "family", "angle", "unit", "pop", "black", "share", "bvap")]
z
Plan Family Angle Unit Pop Black Share Bvap
fewest strip 161 1 177848 82443 46.36 44.77
fewest strip 161 2 178582 81894 45.86 43.96
fewest strip 161 3 177793 79883 44.93 43.77
fewest strip 161 4 177788 79057 44.47 44.23
fewest strip 161 5 177707 78920 44.41 43.50
fewest strip 161 6 176992 75427 42.62 40.98
most split 165 1 177998 137188 77.07 76.48
most split 165 2 177718 98510 55.43 54.59
most split 165 3 177806 96558 54.31 51.22
most split 165 4 177590 92142 51.88 49.01
most split 165 5 177826 29724 16.72 16.31
most split 165 6 177772 23502 13.22 12.83

The strip rule at 161 degrees puts all 6 units between 42.6% and 46.4% — every one of them within a couple of points of the county’s own 44.78%, and none of them a majority. That is cracking, arrived at with no intent at all: the slabs run across the grain of the county, so each picks up part of the Black south-west and part of the white north.

The split rule at 165 degrees cuts with the grain instead: 13.2% to 77.1%, and 4 of 6 majority-Black.

A ruler and a protractor did this.

Step 8 — But are they districts? The contiguity test

c(plans                       = FN("n_plans"),
  strictly_contiguous_plans   = FN("plans_strict_contig"),
  effectively_contiguous_plans = FN("plans_contig"),
  threshold_pct               = FN("contig_thr"))
#>                        plans    strictly_contiguous_plans 
#>                          360                            0 
#> effectively_contiguous_plans                threshold_pct 
#>                          172                           99
table(effectively_contiguous = sm$largest_piece_pct >= FN("contig_thr"),
      majority_Black_units   = sm$n_majority)
#>                       majority_Black_units
#> effectively_contiguous   0   1   2   3   4
#>                  FALSE   3  10  95  71   9
#>                  TRUE    0   0 132  40   0

Strict contiguity — every block of a unit reachable from every other — is satisfied by 0 plans out of 360, and the reason is not inkblot shapes. Georgia’s block layer gives the Chattahoochee’s bed, the interstate right-of-way and the airport apron blocks of their own, and they share no boundary with the land across them. Any cut anywhere strands a few near-empty blocks.

So the criterion with meaning is whether a unit’s people form one connected mass. Requiring 99% of every unit’s population in a single piece keeps 172 plans — and among them the answer still runs 2 to 3 majority-Black units. The most extreme plans do not survive; the ambiguity does. On a 6-seat board that is one seat, a sixth of the government, decided by which respectable rule you used.

pu[pu$plan %in% c("fewest_contig", "most_contig"),

Plan Family Angle Unit Pop Share Bvap Pct largest
fewest_contig split 14 1 178135 85.74 84.90 100.00
fewest_contig split 14 2 177636 85.53 85.21 99.92
fewest_contig split 14 3 177644 44.62 43.11 100.00
fewest_contig split 14 4 177756 22.45 21.74 99.96
fewest_contig split 14 5 177951 17.39 17.06 99.99
fewest_contig split 14 6 177588 12.86 12.27 99.99
most_contig strip 86 1 177793 88.15 87.33 100.00
most_contig strip 86 2 176990 83.27 82.50 100.00
most_contig strip 86 3 178516 50.21 46.98 100.00
most_contig strip 86 4 177542 18.69 18.10 99.94
most_contig strip 86 5 177887 17.01 17.54 99.98
most_contig strip 86 6 177982 11.49 11.04 100.00

Step 9 — What you can now say

You can say that a unit’s Black share is a joint fact about the population and the unit, and give the size of the effect: 37.9 points of spread across blocks, 0.0 across the county.

You can say that aggregation destroys tails, and by how much: the share of Black Georgians in a majority-Black unit falls from 66.3% to 34.8% between blocks and counties, with nobody moving.

You can say that a correlation is a property of the grouping, and point to one that changes sign.

You can say that the zoning effect is real and large: 6 equal units, 360 race-blind ways of drawing them, 0–4 majority-Black units, still 2–3 once ill-shaped plans go.

You cannot say that any of these is the plan Fulton should have. Nothing here optimises anything. The point is not that one of the 360 is right; it is that “what is the Black share of a district here?” has 360 answers before anyone has argued about anything.

Your turn

Change one thing, re-run, and write about what changed. Pick one.

Option A — A different county. data/ga_block_race.csv holds all 232,717 Georgia blocks. Change the five-character county GEOID from Fulton’s 13121 to another county and rebuild the scale ladder. Chatham (13051), Dougherty (13095), Forsyth (13117) and Clayton (13063) are usefully different from each other. Does the scale effect bite harder or softer than in Fulton, and what does that tell you about the spatial scale of segregation there?

Option B — A different definition of “Black.” The ladder uses black_any. Rebuild it with black_alone and report what moves and what does not. Which statistic is most sensitive to the definition — the mean, the spread, or the count of majority-Black units? Which choice would you defend in court?

Option C — A different threshold. Fifty percent is a legal convention, not a natural constant. Using data/zoning_sweep.csv, recount how many units of each plan clear 40%, 45%, 55% and 60%, and do it with bvap (voting-age) as well as share (total population). At which threshold does the choice of plan stop mattering — and why is that the interesting number?

Option D — Your own question. 360 partitions, 232,717 blocks, four rungs of census geography.

What this lab cannot tell you

  • Whether any real plan was drawn to do this. Nothing here has intent. The lab shows the zoning effect is available, not that it was used.
  • The true range of possible outcomes. Two rule families are not the space of all equal-population partitions. 0–4 is a lower bound on the ambiguity, not the answer.
  • Anything about voters. These are residents. Fulton is 44.78% Black by population and 43.51% by voting-age population, and neither is turnout.
  • Anything about individuals. Aggregating race to areas and reasoning down to people is the ecological fallacy; see levels-of-aggregation, and see rpv for the one place in this course where the inference can be checked against an answer key.
  • How much of the block counts is noise. The 2020 census injects differential-privacy noise, and it matters more at block level than at county level — which is itself a scale effect.

On the discussion board

By Friday, 11:59 p.m.

  • Step 6 shows two rules that cannot see race producing 0 and 4 majority-Black units. What, if anything, does “the algorithm is race-blind” establish?
  • Step 4 shows a correlation changing sign between blocks and counties. If you read a study reporting a correlation across counties, what is the one question you now have to ask?
  • Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act asks whether a minority group is “sufficiently large and geographically compact” to constitute a majority in a district. After this lab, is that a question about people, about maps, or about both — and who should get to answer it?

Where the data came from

  • Race by census block — U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File, legacy format, Georgia; tables P1 (total population by race) and P3 (voting-age population by race). This is the file the Bureau is required by law to deliver to every state legislature so it can draw districts. https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Georgia/ga2020.pl.zip
  • Block, block group and tract boundaries — Census TIGER/Line 2020, Georgia. https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2020/BG/tl_2020_13_bg.zip and https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2020/TRACT/tl_2020_13_tract.zip; blocks (tl_2020_13_tabblock20) are shared with ga-precinct-returns.
  • Interior points — the Bureau’s own INTPTLAT20/INTPTLON20, the same idea as assignPolys in Cervas, R-Functions. https://github.com/jcervas/R-Functions/tree/main/assignPolys
  • The concept — Openshaw, S. (1984), The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem, CATMOG 38; Robinson, W. S. (1950), “Ecological Correlations and the Behavior of Individuals,” American Sociological Review 15(3).

Builds are in data/: build-block-race.R reads the P.L. 94-171 file into ga_block_race.csv (232,717 blocks, 10,711,908 people); build-areal-units.R produces the ladders, the maps and the 360 partitions. Both record their source URLs, fetch date and row counts, and both stop if a GEOID is not the width it should be.
